e.etymology: A respelling of Naomi that follows the nye-OH-mee pronunciation. Naomi is Hebrew No'omi, pleasantness; in the Bible she is the mother-in-law of Ruth.
An English surname from places named Colston, joining the Old Norse personal name Kolr with Old English tun, settlement. US use rose around 2010 with Saints receiver Marques Colston.
e.note: In Britain the name recalls Edward Colston, the slave trader whose Bristol statue was toppled in 2020.

e.etymology: A joining of Anna, from Hebrew Hannah, grace, and Leah, the first wife of Jacob in the Bible. It sounds close to the Spanish name Analia.

e.meaning: varies by kanji: lovely, courtesy, bell-like chime
e.etymology: A Japanese name for girls and boys whose meaning depends on the characters chosen, such as lovely, courtesy or the chime of jewels. A separate Hebrew Rei, my friend, is a supporter of King David in the Bible.
namesakes: Rei Kawakubo (founder of Comme des Garcons)

assoc.t: REI, the outdoor gear retailer, same spelling
Rey, heroine of the Star Wars sequels, by sound
Rei Ayanami, pilot in Neon Genesis Evangelion
Rei Hino, Sailor Mars in Sailor Moon

e.note: On paper it matches REI, the outdoor retailer; rei is also Portuguese for king.

e.etymology: A modern American name that joins Jah, a short form of God's name in the Bible and in Rastafari, to the sound of Nasir and Yasir.
A recent name with no settled origin. It is found as a Turkish and Kurdish name, and it sits close in sound to Aiden, Dylan and Ayla.
e.note: Aylan Kurdi was the name reported for the Syrian toddler whose 2015 drowning became a symbol of the refugee crisis.

e.etymology: A modern American coinage in the style of Bexley, Brinley and Paisley, with the -ley ending of English place names. It has no meaning of its own.
A respelling of Haisley, a surname turned first name that caught on in the 2010s on the pattern of Paisley and Hadley.
A respelling of Lennox, a Scottish surname from the district of Lennox near Loch Lomond, whose Gaelic name refers to elm trees. The -yx ending echoes Onyx and Nyx.

assoc.t: Lennox heating and air conditioning, by sound
Lenox china and tableware, by sound

e.etymology: A respelling of Rustin, a surname used as a first name. It shares its sound with Rusty, the old nickname for someone with red hair, and takes the -yn ending of Austyn.
A recent blend of Maeve and Mavis. Maeve is the Irish Medb, she who intoxicates, a legendary queen of Connacht; mavis is an old word for the song thrush.
The Danish and Norwegian form of Christina, a contraction of Kristine, recorded in Denmark since the 1100s. Christina comes from Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
namesakes: Kirsten Gillibrand (US senator from New York)

assoc.t: Kirsten Larson, pioneer-era American Girl doll

e.etymology: A German name from Old High German heri, army, and wini, friend, popular in the early 1900s. In English it has also been used as a variant of Irwin.
namesakes: Erwin Schrodinger (physicist of the cat thought experiment)
Erwin Rommel (German field marshal of World War II)

assoc.t: Erwin Smith, commander in Attack on Titan

e.etymology: The French form of Alfonso, a name the Visigoths brought to Spain, from Germanic words for noble and ready. It was the name of many kings of Spain and Portugal.
A feminine form of Joel, from Hebrew Yo'el, the Lord is God, also read as Jo joined to Ella. It has been on US birth records since the 1880s.

e.meaning: of Mars, the Roman god of war
e.etymology: From Latin Marcellina, the feminine of Marcellinus, which builds on Marcellus and Marcus, names tied to the god Mars. Saint Marcellina was the sister of Saint Ambrose.
The Russian and Ukrainian pet form of Yekaterina and Kateryna, the equivalents of Katherine. Katherine is Greek Aikaterine, long associated with katharos, pure.
namesakes: Katya Zamolodchikova (drag star of RuPaul's Drag Race)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins the Jav- of Javier and Javon with the -ian ending of Darian and Julian. It has no meaning of its own.
A less common spelling of Lilia, from Latin lilia, the plural of lilium, lily, or a Latin-style form of the English Lily. It was in fashion in the US in the 1890s.

assoc.t: Lillia, a champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: In Finnish, Jori is a men's form of George, from Greek georgos, farmer. In the US it is mostly a girls' name, a short form in the family of Jordan and Marjorie, also spelled Jorie and Jory.
A form of Mahala, which goes back to the Biblical names Mahlah and Mahalath and was long used in the American South. Gospel great Mahalia Jackson made this form famous.
A spelling of Anaya with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah and Aniyah. Anaya rose in the US in the 2000s alongside Amaya and Janiya and is also a Spanish surname.

The Hebrew original of Isaac, from the verb to laugh: in Genesis, Sarah laughed when told she would bear a son in old age. This spelling shows the Hebrew sounds and is used in Orthodox Jewish families.
namesakes: Yitzhak Rabin (Israeli prime minister and Nobel peace laureate)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that puts Az- in front of the -lynn ending of Ashlynn and Adalynn. It has no meaning of its own.
A pet form of Pessel or Pesha, Yiddish women's names whose origin is debated. It is used mainly in Hasidic Jewish communities.
From Hawaiian kaimana, 'diamond', a word borrowed from English. It can also be read as kai, 'sea', plus mana, 'power': a powerful sea.
The Arabic name of Luqman the Wise, a sage whose advice to his son fills the 31st chapter of the Quran, which is named for him. The source of the name itself is not known.
From Sanskrit yuvan, 'young' or 'a youth', a distant relative of Latin juvenis and English young.
From Hebrew zemirah, 'song'. In the Bible Zemirah is a man of the tribe of Benjamin listed in 1 Chronicles; in modern use it is a girls' name.
A Latin American spelling of Angely or Angeli, written the way the soft English g sounds to a Spanish speaker. The source is Angela, from Greek angelos, 'messenger'.
From Arabic taym, 'servant' or 'one enthralled by love', an old Arab name. Banu Taym was the clan of Abu Bakr, the first caliph.
The German, Scandinavian and South Slavic spelling of Sonya, a Russian pet form of Sofiya, from Greek sophia, 'wisdom'.
namesakes: Sonja Henie (Norwegian Olympic figure skater and film star)
